<reason>B won the decisive timing clash. A established harms from surprise charges and unseen restrictions, but insufficiently justified banning an obligation-free checkout review when honest totals and suitability restrictions already appear earlier. B answered both pressure questions with enforceable safeguards rather than voluntary restraint. A repeatedly attacked concealment that B expressly prohibited. Its bright-line defense also failed to resolve B’s points that pressure can occur before checkout, conspicuousness still requires judgment, and staged disclosure can improve attention rather than manipulate consumers.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B dismantled A’s “zero cost or confessed manipulation” fork: platforms can stage information because comparison and confirmation serve different tasks. Combined with B’s honest-total requirement, this preserved a legitimate review workflow without reproducing A’s surprise-price example. A ultimately conceded that the click itself could be harmless.</best_rebuttal>
